claims.text: Pulumi's component state migrations feature is new and lets component authors ship an upgrade path with the component itself.
A Pulumi component state migration translates the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi works out which resources need to change (i.e., before the engine computes the diff/plan).
The Pulumi component state migrations API is experimental and may change.
A GitHub discussion for component state migrations feedback exists at github.com/pulumi/pulumi/discussions/24799.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ (component state migrations guide) that covers the callback contract.
The pulumi/examples repository contains an example directory aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration with three programs (v1, v2, v3) and the migration code, and a README for v1.
The pulumi/examples repo contains migration files at aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts and v3/migration.ts.

Pulumi components let you turn a group of resources into a reusable building block, with users working with inputs and outputs without needing to understand every resource inside; docs at /docs/iac/concepts/components/.
The legacy AWSX VPC component (`awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc`) manages the VPC, subnets, route tables, and gateways.

In the example's v1, the legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component creates a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and its association, and an internet gateway; a security group sits outside the component and refers to the VPC.
Because the security group refers to the VPC's ID, replacing the VPC would require replacing the security group too (per AWS CloudFormation EC2 SecurityGroup VpcId documentation).
Without a migration connecting old state to new code, upgrading from the legacy to modern AWSX VPC component could replace the VPC instead of keeping it.
If a database is recreated, its replacement does not automatically contain the old data; deleting the old database without a backup or data migration could lose that data.
The example does not create a database.
The example's second version upgrades to the modern `awsx.ec2.Vpc` component while keeping the existing network.
The example's third version removes AWSX and declares the resources directly with `@pulumi/aws`.
Across all three versions of the example, the AWS resource IDs stay the same and the security group continues to use the same VPC.

In the example, the Pulumi resource tree for v1 is awsx:x:ec2:Vpc with children aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc, awsx:x:ec2:Subnet (containing subnet, routeTable, routeTableAssociation named vpc-isolated-0) and awsx:x:ec2:InternetGateway (containing aws InternetGateway); v2 is awsx:ec2:Vpc containing aws Vpc with subnet, routeTable, association (vpc-isolated-1) and internet gateway; v3 is aws Vpc as root with those beneath.
Pulumi's state records both physical resources and the components that group them; each record has a Pulumi name called a URN, and managed resources also have a provider ID.
Legacy AWSX wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate components; modern AWSX removes those wrappers and places the managed resources under different parents.
In the example, the Pulumi name of the subnet changes from `vpc-isolated-0` to `vpc-isolated-1` between legacy and modern AWSX.

Pulumi aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible, but cannot by themselves remove component wrappers and transfer references to replacement resources; a state migration describes that whole change together.
Pulumi resource options accept a `stateMigrations` option that registers migration callbacks, and a component can be registered with an alias for the legacy component type.
With a state migration, the alias lets Pulumi find the old component and the callback receives its saved state followed by the state of its children.

A state migration callback returns `newState` (the complete set of records replacing the old component and its children) and `successors` (a map from each old URN that disappears to the URN that takes its place).
In the example migration callback, an unexpected component type raises an error, and the callback is idempotent: if state already uses modern AWSX or plain AWS resources, it does nothing.
The example's `rename` helper copies the saved record and changes its URN, type, and parent, preserving the AWS resource ID and other saved fields.

Pulumi uses the `successors` mappings to update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack, so the security group's reference to the VPC remains valid after migration and keeps the same AWS VPC ID.
The example's second migration removes the AWSX VPC component record and maps both the old component and its VPC child to the new VPC record, which keeps its AWS ID.

Pulumi runs multiple state migration callbacks in order, passing each result to the next callback; a stack on legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to plain AWS, a stack on modern AWSX skips the first migration, and after both have run, both callbacks return no result on later updates.

After a migration changes saved state, Pulumi compares the new program with that state and calls the provider for remaining changes; this example can still show in-place updates for provider defaults and tags.

During upgrade between example versions, `pulumi preview` should show no creates, deletes, or replacements for the existing VPC, subnet, route table, association, internet gateway, and security group.
`pulumi preview` evaluates the state migration without saving it, and `pulumi up` saves the migrated state.

When a component author registers the migration inside the component implementation, users do not need to write the migration, attach the callback, or edit stack state; Pulumi runs the migration as part of normal preview and update.
For an internal component change that keeps the same inputs and outputs, users can keep their existing component calls unchanged.
Pulumi's state migration callbacks (the `stateMigrations` resource option) run during both previews and updates when prior state exists for the resource.
Pulumi state migration callbacks (the `stateMigrations` resource option) must be idempotent.
A state migration callback must return no result when the resource's state no longer needs migration.
State migration callbacks rewrite resource state without performing any provider operations.
A Pulumi component state migration is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.
A component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings.
Each successor mapping returned by a component state migration callback connects an old URN that is omitted from the result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
If no migration is needed, a component state migration callback returns no result.
The Pulumi option reference at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/statemigrations/#callback-api explains the state migration callback API.

Component state migration callback state entries use the checkpoint resource format documented in the Pulumi developer docs deployment schema (pulumi-resource-state), including fields such as urn, type, id, parent, provider, inputs, and outputs.
A component state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using Pulumi update plans or targeted updates.
The restrictions on state-changing results of component state migrations (under update plans or targeted updates) do not require removing an already-applied migration.
